The deviation could be a result of assuming 3D random fiber orientation, no defects, porosity and perfect bonding between the metal and polymer composite. The resultant von mises stress and displacement contours from the numerical model are illustrated in Figure 5.3.1.2(c). It is evident from the stress contour that the polymer composite is under low stress and predominantly transfers the load to the metal lattice structure. The metal lattice structure reinforcing the polymer composite thus acts as a load-carrying member. Stress concentration regions were observed in the metal lattice at the edges, intersections, and sharp corners. The numerical model predicted failure of the tensile specimen to occur at one of the stress concentration locations in the neck region as depicted in Figure 5.3.1.3(a) which is in good agreement with the experiments. The fracture morphology from stereomicroscopy revealed that the stress concentration at the edge initiated crack propagation along metal-polymer interface and subsequently caused the metal strut failure as shown in Figure 5.3.1.3(b)- (c). The local stresses exceeding that of yield strength of maraging steel (2400 MPa) continued the crack propagation across the entire neck region causing failure of the tensile specimen. 31 | P age Figure 5.3.1.3. The overmolded metal composite specimen was monitored using DIC system which was synchronized with the tensile testing frame. Two different cameras were used to observe the polymer and metal sides of the overmolded specimens under tension. The initial images and at fracture images obtained from DIC are shown in Fig. 5.3.1. The stress-strain curves obtained from the analysis are shown in Fig. 5.3.1 as well. The stress-strain curves reveal a good agreement between the tracking on either side of the specimens.
